title: The householder's path, closed
hookLine: work, money, family, friends, body, age: one bedside talk holds them all
tomorrow: everyone knows they'll die. so why think about it on purpose?

lines: WHO PAYS? WHO PICKS UP THE KIDS?
A SICK MAN, WORRIED FOR HIS WIFE.
cards: Hospital waiting rooms run on the same quiet talk under the beeping: who pays the bills, who picks up the kids, what happens to the house. An old story sits right inside that talk.
A householder known as Nakula's father lies badly sick, and he isn't worried about dying. He's worried about his wife. Will she manage the money?
The children? Will she marry again? Will she stop going to hear the Buddha?
She leans in close, and answers every worry, one by one.

teach.b: The story is in the Anguttara Nikaya, and it's mostly her talking. Don't die worried, she tells him; the Blessed One says dying with worry is painful.
Then, worry by worry. The money: I'm good at spinning cotton and carding wool; I can keep the children fed. The marriage: you know I won't take another husband.
The teaching: I'll want to see the Buddha and the monks more, not less. And her own practice: she keeps the precepts, she has found calm in her mind, she's gone beyond doubt in the teaching.
If you're unsure, she says, go ask the Blessed One. Then the twist. Nakula's father gets better.

teach.h: HE GETS UP, LEANING ON A STICK.
teach.b: He gets up from his sickbed, still weak, leaning on a stick, and goes to the Buddha himself. The Buddha tells him he's fortunate: Nakula's mother is his counselor and teacher, full of kindness for his good.
Now hold her speech up to the light. Work is in it, the spinning. Money, the children's food.
Family, the marriage. Friends, the community around the Buddha. The body, sick in that bed, and age, the long life they've shared.
Every room of the householder's path is in one bedside talk, and in every room the practice was already there.
Not on a cushion somewhere else. In the cotton, in a promise, in a steady voice next to a frightened man.

how: Buddhist teachers often tell lay students the story of Nakula's parents to show that the path can be walked in married and working life; temples in many countries hold teachings for householders alongside programs for monks and nuns.

o: a monk's path, walked only inside a monastery
the Buddha's path lived in ordinary home life
the road a family takes to a temple festival

games.q: the bedside talk — tap the pairs.
p: she can spin cotton and card wool
she'll see the Buddha more, not less

s: in the story, Nakula's father is afraid of dying for his own sake
his worries are about his wife: the money, the children, the marriage, the teaching.
Nakula's father recovers and goes to see the Buddha himself
still weak, leaning on a stick, he gets up and goes.
real practice happens away from work and family, on a cushion
her practice is in the spinning, the promises and a steady voice. practice is everywhere.

games.q: your dad is laid up after surgery and keeps asking how the family will manage. you're scared too. what does Nakula's mother do in your place?
o: change the subject to something cheerful, so he stops thinking about it.
answer each worry plainly and calmly, one at a time.
tell him worrying is bad for his recovery and he should stop.
games.why: she doesn't dodge or scold. she takes each worry, money, marriage, teaching, and answers it, and the Buddha calls her his counselor and teacher.

practice: Name one room of your life where the practice feels thinnest right now: work, money, family, friends, or the body. Bring to mind one ordinary moment there this week, the hard email or the tense dinner.
Then choose one small thing to carry into it, a breath before you answer or a gentler word, and rest with that choice until the bell.

wordCard.voice: The householder's path: the Buddha's teaching lived inside work, money, family, friends, body and age, not away from them. Today it closes.

orig.note: Pali: householder, the head of a household; the word the suttas use for lay followers like Nakula's father.

carryVoice: Your line: practice is everywhere, even beside a sickbed. A new stretch of the path begins tomorrow. Day sixteen twenty-five, closed.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.16 (Nakulapita Sutta: Nakula's mother answers her sick husband's worries; he recovers and the Buddha praises her)
